title: David Choe Returns to Cartoonist Kayfabe!
summary: David Choe joins Cartoonist Kayfabe from a parked car on new-comics day and thanks Ed Piskor and Jim Rugg for restoring his comics community. The conversation moves through Geof Darrow, Baron Storey, art school, influence and copying, Gaza/Congo self-report, family finance, forgery, dangerous billboard work, Asian-American categorization, Giant Robot, VICE fabrication, New York comics culture, adult-magazine illustration, false female bylines, poverty, a defective car, Blow, Johnny Depp, Paul Reubens, DVDASA at Comic-Con, collector prices, endings, Slow Jams, stand-up, podcast extremity, guest deletion requests, mental-health treatment, unreleased work, Bourdain, Black Market, comics economics, adult collecting, graffiti archives, intimate-image exchange, P.O.-box watching, impersonated sexual letters, letters pages, unmade collaborations and collection disorder. Every idea and publisher mask remains. Direct refusals, false identities, source-reliability admissions, crew warnings and guest regret remain attached to their sequences. The interview ends after a video failure near 96:28; publisher promotion begins around 97:01. No line-level speaker names are published.

connections.relationship: Choe frames Kayfabe as a preservation service and social bridge rather than only entertainment.
The Darrow friendship and altered-hand experiment lead directly into the separate Darrow/Choe Kayfabe conversation.
Choe repeats the diagnostic reading of Darrow's marks later challenged by Darrow's concrete craft explanation.
Storey anchors Choe's pedagogy, risk tolerance, layered materials and permission to leave school.
The Gaza/Intifada/Congo sequence needs reconciliation with other travel accounts and historical dates.
The family-store fire belongs within wider 1992 Black/Korean, policing and structural history.
The admitted signature forgery begins a long episode pattern of deception disclosed after the fact.
Storey's warning directly counters romantic interpretation of Choe's billboard danger.
Giant Robot supplies the foundational audience that Choe says later mainstream endorsements expanded.
Choe explicitly says several VICE articles mixed truth with invention under false names.
The fabricated female adult-magazine persona anticipates later fake-woman letters to cartoonists.
The leaking-brake and theft sequence preserves risk to strangers rather than romanticizing poverty.
Depp's refusal controls; later Reubens contact cannot retroactively authorize the separate gift.
The Arquette callback and Comic-Con episode connect this source to the mobile DVDASA archive.
Choe claims early Rogan and Kevin Smith appearances were removed, requiring catalog and mirror verification.
The Xeric history explains Choe's ending philosophy and reluctance to dilute a completed work.
Choe says reality ambiguity was an intentional design goal of the show.
The claim that nearly every guest requested deletion is central evidence for per-episode consent review.
The alleged successor-show invitation connects Thumbs Up, travel interviewing and later production rejection.
Choe's origin claim must remain beside Michael K. Williams's released authorship and production records.
The intimate-image-for-caps exchange shows how scene history can conceal nonconsensual exploitation.
P.O.-box watching crosses admiration into surveillance and must not become discovery guidance.
The fabricated Asian-woman letters repeat the earlier adult-magazine deception in a fan context.
Choe chooses friendship over a Darrow project, paralleling the unmade Kayfabe comic request.

source_notes.claim: Known participants make every line safely nameable.
source_notes.assessment: They do not; captions have no prefixes and contain overlap, quotation, a phone break and publisher ads.

source_notes.claim: Art style or output diagnoses OCD, trauma or autism.
source_notes.assessment: It does not; Choe explicitly calls the inference projection and no clinical evaluation exists.

source_notes.claim: The caption's 1994–95 event is the First Intifada.
source_notes.assessment: Standard history dates the First Intifada primarily 1987–93; Choe's place/event chronology requires a primary travel source.

source_notes.claim: One family account explains the Los Angeles uprising.
source_notes.assessment: It does not; broader Black/Korean, policing, Latasha Harlins and structural history is required.

source_notes.claim: Ninety percent of art students fail to earn tuition back.
source_notes.assessment: This is a teacher's reported warning, not verified cohort outcome data.

source_notes.claim: Early Choe/VICE articles are reliable biography because they were published.
source_notes.assessment: Choe says several were partly invented and used false bylines; independent corroboration is mandatory.

source_notes.claim: Repeatedly adding brake fluid made the car safe.
source_notes.assessment: It did not; the account describes an active leak and acknowledged danger to others, requiring professional repair and no driving.

source_notes.claim: Later celebrity contact changes an earlier refusal.
source_notes.assessment: It does not; Depp's reported refusal and Reubens's separate privacy remain controlling.

source_notes.claim: Reading or collecting explicit comics proves child abuse.
source_notes.assessment: It does not; legal status and content require source/jurisdiction review, while offending cannot be inferred from fandom alone.

source_notes.claim: Recording a DVDASA appearance established durable publication consent.
source_notes.assessment: Choe reports widespread immediate deletion requests; each source needs its own edit/publication evidence.

source_notes.claim: Acting in Beef caused a particular psychiatric condition.
source_notes.assessment: The source supplies temporal self-report only; it does not establish diagnosis or causation.

source_notes.claim: Bourdain definitively commissioned Choe as his successor.
source_notes.assessment: This is Choe's account of development interest and a later company rejection, not a completed commission.
His pilot/origin claim requires production records and must not displace Michael K. Williams's released work and collaborators.

source_notes.claim: Superhero films never grow comics readership.
source_notes.assessment: The categorical claim requires sales, library and readership data and cannot be established by one store anecdote.

source_notes.claim: A girlfriend's nude image could be traded by the letter writer.
source_notes.assessment: No; the depicted person must consent to creation and distribution, and the archive must never seek or surface the images.

source_notes.claim: Red Room sales and historical prices are current audited commerce.
source_notes.assessment: They are conversational historical claims and require publisher/store records before display.

speaker_policy.status: all line-level turns unresolved; named turns withheld
speaker_policy.reason: The visible episode establishes Ed Piskor, Jim Rugg and David Choe as participants, but the 2,527 automatic-caption segments contain no publisher prefixes and include overlap, quotation, a phone interruption, media references, producer copy, technical failure and a long promotional outro. Names, topic ownership, adjacency and grammar cannot prove every line. Only independently held-out, non-overlapping acoustic/video validation may support named turns.
